Who is upstream, who depends, and where a dam is the lever.

1 · World

Every shared river is on this map. Brighter shading is river water, strongest where that water reaches and fading across dry land, and each cyan arrow runs from a key dam downstream to the people who depend on it. A red stroke means the water was cut off, a dashed stroke means a cut-off was threatened, and clicking a basin opens it.

2 · River basins

One river at a time, with the countries around it. Brighter shading is river water, strongest where that water reaches and fading across dry land, and the cyan arrow runs from a key dam downstream to the people who depend on it. A red stroke means the water was cut off, a dashed stroke means a cut-off was threatened, and the dim blue land shows where the basin sits.

Basin

From the record

The most water-dependent states have never had their water cut off. Cut-offs follow a political break.1, 6

Every state cut-off on record happened while a water treaty was in force.3, 6

The charts behind these lines

Every cut-off came after a break: Partition, terror attacks, Taliban rule, the invasion of Ukraine.

Why a dependent state may be spared

A very dependent state may be spared because cutting it would mean war.

What a treaty does not stop

Treaties exist where disputes exist, and may cap how much can be cut.

Sources and notes
  1. FAO AQUASTAT dependency ratio (variable 4192) and dam capacity (variable 4197). The dependency figure is national, not basin-specific. The inflow diagram omits aquifers for that reason. data.apps.fao.org/aquastat
  2. WRI Aqueduct 4.0 country rankings, baseline and 2050 business-as-usual stress categories. files.wri.org/aqueduct/aqueduct-4-0-country-rankings.zip
  3. Transboundary Freshwater Diplomacy Database, College of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Sciences, Oregon State University. Treaties (February 2023) and the 2024 spatial database of basin outlines. Product of the Transboundary Freshwater Diplomacy Database, College of Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Sciences, Oregon State University. transboundarywaters.ceoas.oregonstate.edu/spatial-datasets
  4. IGRAC and UNESCO-IHP (2025), Transboundary Aquifers of the World, CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO. Hatched shapes are aquifers. doi.org/10.58154/yb8g-cp97
  5. Global Dam Watch database v1.0 (Lehner et al. 2024), CC BY 4.0. Triangles mark dams with at least 1 km³ of storage. doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.25988293
  6. Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology. A coloured line on an arrow is a cut-off or a threat only when this record names both the upstream and the downstream country. A red dam name is a conflict record. worldwater.org/water-conflict
  7. Natural Earth 1:50m countries and 1:10m rivers and lakes, public domain. Shapes are simplified. naturalearthdata.com
  8. Blue Nile share of Nile flow, about four sevenths at Aswan: Awulachew et al., IWMI Working Paper 127 (2008). iwmi.cgiar.org/…/WOR127.pdf
  9. The arrow follows the river from a key dam to sourced downstream places. It is the river course, not a line drawn across land. Arrow starts and the main river, country and dam labels are placed by hand. Other names appear on hover. Dam coordinates follow source 5. Place names on that line are only places already listed for the basin: Khartoum and Lake Nasser on the Nile, and each basin's river, lake and country points. Cairo, Aswan city and the Nile Delta are not given coordinates here, so the Nile line stops at the sourced points.
  10. US–Mexico 1944 water treaty and the 2020 occupation of La Boquilla Dam. Brookings, “Not dried up: US-Mexico water cooperation” (2020), brookings.edu. Reuters (September 2020), reuters.com.
  11. HydroSHEDS HydroRIVERS v1.0 (Lehner and Grill 2013). Average discharge is DIS_AV_CMS, in cubic metres per second. Lines are the reaches inside each basin, simplified. hydrosheds.org/products/hydrorivers
  12. Utrecht Law Review, “Human Right to Water in the Helmand Basin” (2020). On Article 5 of the 1973 Afghan–Iranian Helmand treaty: Afghanistan is not to take any action to deprive Iran totally or partially of its water right. utrechtlawreview.org/articles/10.36633/ulr.566
